blocks.text: INNNNEWS - Dedicates the day of Pancasila's birth on June 1st, the intortion is happening again in this nation. Recent cases have been reported in Bantul, Yogyakarta special area. The community congregation of the mission church (GMS) was disbanded by a group of mob on behalf of the people's permission and rejection.

Ironically, the act took place in front of the security authorities who were judged not to make a decisive move to stop intimidation. Amnesty International Indonesia calls this a state-run violation of religious freedom.

This phenomenon is not a single event. In recent years, the denial of the temple has been repeated in many areas. The administrative issue is often legitimized to limit the rights of worshipping minority groups.

Whereas, the constitution through Article 29 UUD 1945 clearly ensures the freedom of each citizen to embrace religion and worship their own beliefs. When the mob can determine who to worship and who not to worship, then the country is indeed losing its power.

The problem becomes more serious because intolerance is no longer just targeting religions, but also ethnic identities. Recently the public is talking about the alleged rejection of Chinese students or Chindo students in the paskibraka local selection.

The narratives on social media call the participants being questioned because of their ethnic identity and the area language skills. Despite the fact that it still needs to be verified, this poll shows that stereotypes against Chinese ethnicities are still living in the midst of Indonesian society.

In fact, the Chinese are a legitimate part of Indonesia. They're born, they grow, they go to school, they work and they contribute in this country. However, stigma is not a natural state that still comes in many forms of social discrimination and politics. This kind of issue has been the alarm that the Indonesian inclusiveness spirit is not fully cooked.

The Paskibraka case also touched important symbolic issues. Paskibraka is not just a ceremonial activity, but a symbol of nationalism and representation of the young generation of Indonesia. If ethnic identity is still a matter of rejection, then the unification in state ceremonies becomes contradictory. The state seems to have failed to ensure that all citizens have equal positions in public space.

The most alarming thing is the impression that the law only applies when it's not dealing with mass pressure. In the case of the dissolution of the church in Bantul, authorities are considered to be busier to maintain a workaholic trust than to uphold the constitutional rights of citizens. As a result, the intolerant group feels it has room to act because it's sure that the state won't really grant strict sanctions.

If these conditions continue to be left alone, people will lose faith in the law. Minority citizens feel insecure, and intolerant groups feel that their actions are justified. In the long run, this situation could ruin the foundations of Indonesian democracy that are built on the principles of civil equality.

Therefore, the state should re-demonstrate its legal authority. Law enforcement against intolerance should not be half-hearted. The local government, the security authorities, and the law enforcement institutions must stand above the constitution, not bow to the pressure of certain groups. Also, tolerance education needs to be amplified so that young people understand that diversity is not a threat, but the identity of the Indonesian nation itself.

Indonesia does not lack legal rules about religious freedom and antidiscrimination. What is lacking is the courage to uphold it consistently. When the law is defeated by mass intimidation and identity prejudice, then that collapse is not just a sense of safety of minority groups, but also the state's leadership in the eyes of its own people.
